results.claim: Your own hand feels less ticklish than someone else's.
results.evidence: Source 1: "when a person touches 'ticklish' parts on their own body no tickling sensation is experienced."

results.claim: Other people can surprise you, but your own hand cannot.
results.evidence: Source 1: "one cannot surprise, deceive, and thereby tickle oneself."

results.claim: In one MRI study, people used a joystick to control a tickling robot and still could not make themselves laugh.
results.evidence: Source 1: "In 1998, Blakemore and colleagues analyzed the 'self-tickle' response by using MRI technology... When subjects used a joystick to control a 'tickling robot', they could not make themselves laugh."

results.claim: When you move your hand, the cerebellum predicts the contact and tells the somatosensory cortex what to expect.
results.evidence: Source 1: "when a person tries to tickle themselves, the cerebellum sends to the somatosensory cortex... precise information on the position of the tickling target and therefore what sensation to expect."

results.claim: An unknown cortical mechanism then reduces the tickle response.
results.evidence: Source 1: "Apparently an unknown cortical mechanism then decreases or inhibits the tickling sensation."

results.claim: One proposed benefit is that light touch acts as a "non-self detector," helping guard against foreign objects.
results.evidence: Source 1: "knismesis serves as a 'non-self detector' and protects the subject against foreign objects."

results.claim: Ticklish areas may prompt protection of vulnerable spots.
results.evidence: Source 1: "J. C. Gregory proposed that the most ticklish places on the body were also those areas that were the most vulnerable during hand-to-hand combat. He posited that ticklishness might confer an evolutionary advantage by enticing the individual to protect these areas."

results.claim: The difference between self-tickling and being tickled by another is surprise.
results.evidence: Source 1 supports surprise as a factor ("tickling requires a certain amount of surprise... because tickling oneself produces no unexpected motion on the skin, the response is not activated") but also cites cerebellar prediction of self-produced contact, states "the reasons for the inhibition of the tickling sensation during self-tickling remain unknown," and notes light touch (knismesis) is "not dependent on the element of surprise."
